terms.def: In classical conditioning, the stage where a neutral stimulus is repeatedly paired with an unconditioned stimulus until it triggers a response.
A hormone released in the fight-flight-freeze response that increases heart rate and gets the body ready for action.
The first stage of the General Adaptation Syndrome, when the body detects a stressor and the fight-flight-freeze response starts.
A progressive brain disease where neurons are lost, causing worsening memory loss and other thinking problems.
A small brain structure that processes emotions, especially fear, and helps form emotional memories.
The inability to create mental images in the mind.
In the Transactional Model, the way a person judges a situation, first for threat and then for ability to cope.
Focusing on certain information while ignoring other information. It decides what moves from sensory memory to short-term memory.
Memory of events and facts from your own life.
The part of the peripheral nervous system that controls involuntary body functions, such as heart rate and digestion.
Staying away from a feared object or situation. It stops a person learning that the fear is not needed.
Body-based influences on mental health, such as genes, brain chemicals and physical health.
The brain and spinal cord.
A brain structure at the back of the head that controls balance and coordinates movement. It stores procedural memories.
A body cycle of about 24 hours, such as the sleep-wake cycle, that is controlled by an internal clock.
Learning that happens when a neutral stimulus is paired with an unconditioned stimulus, so it comes to trigger a response by itself.
Relating to mental processes such as thinking, remembering, paying attention and problem-solving.
The learned response to a conditioned stimulus in classical conditioning.
A stimulus that was once neutral but now triggers a response because it was paired with a stimulus that triggers the response naturally.
The process of turning new short-term memories into stable long-term memories.
The group in an experiment that does not get the independent variable, so it can be compared with the experimental group.
The ability to change coping strategies to suit the situation, and to stop strategies that are not working.
An action or thought a person uses to manage the demands of a stressor.
A stress hormone released over a longer time in the stress response. It raises blood sugar and gives the body energy.
A circadian rhythm sleep disorder where a person falls asleep and wakes much later than normal.
The variable that is measured in an experiment to see if it was affected by the change the researcher made.
Stress that is negative and harmful, and that overwhelms a person's ability to cope.
Explicit memory for personal events and experiences, including when and where they happened.
The last stage of the General Adaptation Syndrome, when long-term stress uses up the body's resources and the person is at higher risk of illness.
Long-term memory that you can consciously recall, including episodic and semantic memory.
In classical conditioning, the fading of a conditioned response when the conditioned stimulus is repeatedly presented without the unconditioned stimulus.
A variable other than the independent variable that could affect the results, but is not the one being tested.
The body's automatic response to a threat, preparing a person to fight, run away or stay still.
A treatment for phobias where a person is exposed to the feared object at full strength until the fear reduces.
The main inhibitory neurotransmitter in the brain. It reduces the chance that the next neuron will fire.
Selye's model of the body's response to long-term stress, with three stages: alarm reaction, resistance and exhaustion.
The main excitatory neurotransmitter in the brain. It makes the next neuron more likely to fire.
The community of bacteria and other tiny organisms that live in the gut.
The two-way communication between the gut and the brain, using nerves, hormones and chemical messengers.
A brain structure that is important for forming new explicit long-term memories.
A testable prediction about the relationship between the variables in a study.
Long-term memory that affects behaviour without conscious effort, such as skills and conditioned responses.
The variable that the researcher changes in an experiment to see its effect.
Describes a neurotransmitter that makes the next neuron less likely to fire.
A neuron in the central nervous system that connects sensory neurons to motor neurons.
The memory store with unlimited capacity that holds information for a long time, possibly for life.
A lasting increase in the strength of a synapse after repeated activity, thought to be the basis of learning and memory.
A hormone made by the pineal gland that makes you sleepy. More is released in darkness.
A condition with significant disturbance in thinking, emotion or behaviour that causes distress or problems in daily life.
A state of wellbeing where a person can cope with normal stress, work well and take part in their community.
A memory aid, such as a rhyme or acronym, that helps you remember information.
A neuron that carries messages from the central nervous system to muscles or glands.
Removing an unpleasant stimulus after a behaviour, which makes the behaviour more likely to happen again.
A nerve cell that sends information as electrical and chemical signals.
A chemical messenger released by a neuron that crosses the synapse to affect the next neuron.
A stimulus that does not trigger the response of interest before conditioning.
The sleep stages without rapid eye movement. They include light sleep (stages 1 and 2) and deep sleep (stage 3).
Learning by watching the behaviour of a model and its consequences, then copying it later.
Learning where the likelihood of a behaviour changes because of its consequences, such as reinforcement or punishment.
The part of the autonomic nervous system that calms the body and restores normal function after a stressor.
A person who takes part in a research study.
All the nerves outside the brain and spinal cord, connecting the central nervous system to the rest of the body.
An intense, irrational fear of a specific object or situation that causes distress and avoidance.
A small gland in the brain that releases melatonin.
A fake treatment with no active ingredient, used to check whether results are due to the real treatment.
The whole group of people that a researcher wants to study.
Adding something pleasant after a behaviour, which makes the behaviour more likely to happen again.
The neuron that receives the neurotransmitter across the synapse.
The neuron that sends the neurotransmitter into the synapse.
In the Transactional Model, a person's first judgment of whether a situation is irrelevant, positive or a threat (stressful).
Implicit memory for how to do skills and actions, such as riding a bike.
A consequence that makes a behaviour less likely to happen again.
Putting participants into groups by chance, so each person has an equal chance of being in each group.
Retrieving information from memory without being given cues, such as in a short-answer test.
A fast, automatic response to a stimulus that is processed in the spinal cord without needing the brain first.
Repeating information over and over, which helps keep it in short-term memory and move it to long-term memory.
A consequence that makes a behaviour more likely to happen again.
A sleep stage with rapid eye movements, vivid dreams and an active brain, and a very relaxed body.
The second stage of the General Adaptation Syndrome, when the body tries to cope with a continuing stressor.
Getting stored information out of memory so it can be used.
In the Transactional Model, a person's judgment of whether they have the resources to cope with a stressor.
Explicit memory for general facts and knowledge, such as the capital of a country.
The memory store that holds sensory information for a very short time, less than a few seconds.
A neuron that carries information from the senses or body to the central nervous system.
The memory store with limited capacity and duration that holds information currently being used.
Not getting enough sleep, which can harm mood, attention and thinking.
The time at which a person goes from being awake to being asleep.
The daily pattern of being asleep and being awake, controlled by the circadian rhythm.
Help and care from other people, such as family and friends, that helps a person cope with stress.
The part of the peripheral nervous system that controls voluntary muscle movements and carries sensory information.
A bundle of nerves in the spine that carries messages between the brain and the body, and controls reflexes.
Something in the environment that causes a response.
Anything that causes stress, such as an event, a situation or a demand.
A small area of the hypothalamus that acts as the body's main clock and controls the circadian rhythm.
The part of the autonomic nervous system that prepares the body for action in a stressful situation.
The tiny gap between two neurons where neurotransmitters pass from one to the other.
A treatment for phobias where a person learns relaxation and is exposed to the feared object step by step.

terms.term: Transactional Model of Stress and Coping
terms.def: Lazarus and Folkman's model that says stress depends on how a person appraises a situation and their ability to cope.
A response that happens naturally, without learning, to an unconditioned stimulus.
A stimulus that triggers a response naturally, without any learning.
How well a study measures what it says it measures, and whether its conclusions are correct.
An outside cue, such as light, that helps set the body's internal clock.
